newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African economy counts cost of gold price fall.
newsitem.headline: S.African economy counts cost of gold price fall.

text.p: South Africa, its economy founded on gold, is bracing for a knock from this month's meltdown in the bullion price.
But economists believe the impact on the balance of payments will be moderated due to significant forward sales by gold mines and the shrinking contribution of the yellow metal to overall exports.
"Gold now plays a much smaller part in the economy than in the 1980s and this (gold price fall) reinforces that trend," said Constantin Vayenas, emerging market analyst at UBS in London.
"It is obviously not positive news but it is not the disaster that some people suggest."

Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said last week that if gold stayed at $320 an ounce for a full year, the loss in foreign exchange on the balance of payments would be around 4.5 billion rand ($1 billion), or just under three percent of total exports.
Gold was last trading around $322 an ounce, some $65 below last year's average price, having hit a 12-year low of $314 earlier this month in the wake of fresh central bank sales.
The short-term impact of gold's slump may well be less than $1 billion a year because many mines have locked in better prices via forward sales, delaying the impact of the price fall.

At the same time gold is no longer the mainstay of the economy, contributing just 18 percent to total South African exports of goods and services of over 150 billion rand a year, down from a peak of 50 percent in 1980.
Other sectors of the economy, notably manufacturing, are growing in importance.

"We are expecting a reasonable showing from the manufacturing sector in 1997 which will make up much of the difference. Overall the effect on the balance of payments is not likely to be that serious," said Anastasia Gekis of ABN Amro in Johannesburg.
On the upside, there are also hopes that a slide in gold output-- production hit a 40-year low of 495 tonnes in 1996-- may soon be reversed.
A landmark productivity-linked wage deal with unions, agreed in principle earlier this month, aims to boost output by 90 tonnes a year.

The success of the accord hangs on mine level deals between management and workers. But both sides have had their minds concentrated by the cost-price squeeze which Gekis believes now questions the viability of around 60 percent of all mines.

Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd was the latest to warn of the fallout of current low prices on Thursday, saying it was reviewing all marginal shafts at its Freegold unit, the world's biggest gold mine.
Widespread closures would throw tens of thousands of miners out of work, worsening already serious unemployment problems and triggering a social crisis.

That would deal a body blow to the government's Growth, Employment and Redistribution programme, which is already disappointing on the jobs front after a 1.1 percent fall in employment in 1996 against a targeted 1.3 percent rise.
